section_summary: This section traces U.S. and occupation authorities’ debate over Japanese deconcentration and proposed revisions to the Anti-Monopoly Law in late 1948 and early 1949. Tokyo reports the release of restricted companies, narrowing use of the Deconcentration Law, and negotiations over stockholding and other antitrust rules. The section ends with a list of 142 released firms and the beginning of a lengthy Nippon Soda reorganization order.

subfiles.title: Request for texts of Anti-Monopoly Law proposals
subfiles.from: Department of State, Robert A. Lovett
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department requests texts of proposals to amend Japan’s Anti-Monopoly Law.
subfiles.summary: Requests copies for study in Washington.

subfiles.title: FEC 230
subfiles.from: W. A. Rudlin
subfiles.about: Rudlin considers competing State and Army positions on deconcentration policy.
subfiles.summary: He supports a public statement and message to SCAP but expects Army resistance. He urges Saltzman to convene Nitze and Butterworth and, if necessary, elevate the unresolved policy split.

subfiles.title: Department of State file charge sheet
subfiles.about: A file form records the document date and decimal file number.

subfiles.title: FEC-230
subfiles.from: R. Fearey
subfiles.about: Fearey evaluates Nitze’s conditions for withdrawing FEC 230.
subfiles.summary: He favors a brief FEC statement affirming deconcentration, questions proposals to expand the program to heterogeneous companies and banking, and supports reexamining securities disposal. He recommends a senior meeting and a draft statement.

subfiles.title: Anti-Trust and Deconcentration Policy
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Tokyo reports reconsideration of 175 companies’ stock-disposal obligations and pending antitrust amendments.
subfiles.summary: The Holding Company Liquidation Commission will review the firms under the Deconcentration Review Board’s principles. Sebald suggests that transferring cases to the Fair Trade Commission could delay stock sales until a softened Anti-Monopoly Law takes effect. He describes disagreement over intercorporate holdings and pending test cases.

subfiles.title: Anti-Trust Policy Is Eased by HCLC
subfiles.from: Nippon Times
subfiles.about: A newspaper account describes the planned review of 175 designated concerns.
subfiles.summary: The HCLC will reassess past monopoly conduct and may cancel designations or limit reorganization to stock liquidation.

subfiles.title: Proposed FEC statement on deconcentration
subfiles.from: George F. Kennan
subfiles.about: Kennan recommends shortening a proposed U.S. statement to the Far Eastern Commission.
subfiles.summary: He favors an early, shorter statement and suggests guidance to SCAP before its release.

subfiles.title: Draft Statement to the Far Eastern Commission re Deconcentration
subfiles.from: United States delegation, draft revised by George F. Kennan
subfiles.about: The draft explains U.S. withdrawal of FEC 230 in light of occupation reforms already undertaken.
subfiles.summary: It reviews the dissolution of holding companies, stock divestment, antitrust legislation, banking changes, and Japanese administrative work. It concludes that progress by SCAP and the Japanese government makes another directive unnecessary.

subfiles.title: Routing note on Tokyo despatch 711
subfiles.about: The note forwards Tokyo’s report on releasing restricted firms.
subfiles.summary: Calls SCAP’s relaxation of restrictions on roughly 1,100 concerns realistic and foresighted.

subfiles.title: Prospective Release of Japanese Concerns from Certain SCAP Restrictions
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Tokyo reports a planned easing of transaction restrictions on roughly 1,100 Japanese companies.
subfiles.summary: The restrictions had required approval for asset sales, capital expansion, and loans. Officials judged mass asset disposal unlikely and prolonged surveillance impractical; reparations and restitution controls would remain.

subfiles.title: Texts of proposed Anti-Monopoly Law revisions
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Tokyo answers Washington’s request for texts of proposed antitrust revisions.
subfiles.summary: Earlier drafts are unavailable; the latest Fair Trade Commission proposal is under discussion and will be sent when obtained.

subfiles.title: Release of Japanese Concerns from Certain Restrictions
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Tokyo explains SCAP’s order easing restrictions on approximately 1,000 concerns.
subfiles.summary: SCAP directed repeal of the approval rule for transactions outside normal business while retaining other controls. It also required clarification of rules for successor companies and repeal of a wartime law limiting shareholder authority.

subfiles.title: Regulations Affecting Restricted Concerns
subfiles.from: R. M. Levy, for the Supreme Commander
subfiles.about: SCAP directs changes to ordinances governing restricted companies.
subfiles.summary: Rescinds one permission requirement, clarifies successor-company coverage, and orders repeal of a wartime company law.

subfiles.title: Activity of 1000 Restricted Concerns to Be Increased
subfiles.from: GHQ Far East Command Public Information Office
subfiles.about: SCAP announces removal of prior approval requirements for many restricted companies.
subfiles.summary: Over 1,000 firms gain freedom for rehabilitation and expansion, while divestiture and deconcentration laws remain effective.

subfiles.title: Handwritten query on anti-trust revision
subfiles.about: A handwritten official asks about SCAP’s antitrust revision and possible U.S. action.
subfiles.summary: Asks what SCAP material is available and how Washington can respond.

subfiles.title: Revision of Anti-Trust Laws
subfiles.from: M. Green
subfiles.about: Green responds to questions about SCAP’s antitrust changes and NSC 13/2.
subfiles.summary: He reports no direct SCAP material and argues that NSC 13/2 wrongly assumes SCAP resists reform changes and that Japanese officials initiate revisions. He doubts Washington can prescribe detailed adjustments.

subfiles.title: Attached despatch 734
subfiles.from: R. Fearey
subfiles.about: Fearey proposes a response to SCAP involvement in Japanese antitrust revisions.
subfiles.summary: He suggests a wire emphasizing Japanese discretion under NSC 13/2 and requesting proposed changes for information. He opposes detailed U.S. instructions.

subfiles.title: Attached Tokyo’s 734
subfiles.from: M. Green
subfiles.about: Green comments on proposed Anti-Trust Law amendments and occupation influence.
subfiles.summary: He notes emerging agreement over intercorporate holdings but argues that GHQ still drives Japanese economic legislation. Japanese agencies and political groups differ over the reforms.

subfiles.title: Revision of Anti-Monopoly Law
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Tokyo forwards the Fair Trade Commission’s latest proposed Anti-Monopoly Law amendments.
subfiles.summary: Sebald describes compromise provisions on stockholdings, foreign contracts, directorships, mergers, reporting, and enforcement. He notes that prior drafts were withheld and that Edward Welsh’s Washington visit was postponed.

subfiles.title: Proposed Amendment of the Anti-Monopoly Law
subfiles.from: Nakayama Kikumatsu, Fair Trade Commission
subfiles.to: E. C. Welsh and L. N. Salwin
subfiles.about: The Commission submits a replacement draft of antitrust amendments.
subfiles.summary: Says the draft incorporates recent discussions and invites further comments.

subfiles.title: Draft proposed amendments to the Anti-Monopoly Law
subfiles.from: Japanese Fair Trade Commission
subfiles.about: The draft revises rules on concerted activity, contracts, corporate holdings, directors, mergers, and enforcement.
subfiles.summary: Proposed articles prohibit substantial restraints of trade while allowing exceptions for insignificant competitive effects. They set reporting and permission rules for international agreements, share acquisitions, concurrent directorships, and mergers, and give the Fair Trade Commission powers to order violations remedied.

subfiles.title: Anti-Trust and Deconcentration Policy
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Tokyo reports cancellation of company designations and the narrowing of deconcentration proceedings.
subfiles.summary: The HCLC released Nippon Soda, Nissan Chemical, three steel companies, and 142 firms formerly subject to stock disposal. Sebald expects further releases and says the Review Board’s four principles have effectively narrowed the law. He describes shortened hearings, remaining cases, labor objections, and the possibility of voluntary corporate reorganization.

subfiles.title: List of 142 firms released from designation
subfiles.from: Holding Company Liquidation Commission
subfiles.about: The enclosure lists companies released from designation under the Deconcentration Law.
subfiles.summary: Lists 142 firms previously freed from reorganization designation but still listed for stock disposal.

subfiles.title: Final Order Approving Voluntary Reorganization Plan of Nippon Soda
subfiles.from: Holding Company Liquidation Commission; Tadao Sasayama
subfiles.about: The Commission approves a plan to divide and dissolve Nippon Soda.
subfiles.summary: The final order confirms an earlier proposed order with a modification concerning two successor firms. The attached plan creates six independent companies, assigns plants, mines, assets, liabilities, directors and auditors, and sets rules for patents, trademarks, share distribution, taxes, and liquidation. The Commission finds Nippon Soda an excessive concentration and orders implementation. The order continues beyond page 289.
